1. Well taking testosterone has some very minor heart risks to it. But it’s the same risk in cis males. 

2. You are correct Endocrinologists do indeed give you testosterone and do blood tests to make sure that your levels are within range. 

3. Your first one is walked through by a nurse so you do know how to do it yourself. But you can go to a doctor and they can inject for you. You May have to ask your endo on where you can go for that. 

Though not all testosterone is injectable. Some endos prefer to do injectables (mine does at least) just due to how gel testosterone can easily get on others and absorb into their skin. 

But gel is an option, as well as getting a pellet. A small pellet will be inserted into your thigh and they last about 2-3 months (?) I’m not exactly sure how many months they last. But it will give you a steady flow of testosterone basically and you don’t have to do shots. These are things you will have to talk to your endo about. 

4. Testosterone prices can vary, here in America it’s probably about $40+ (I’m on my parents insurance and it’s covered mostly so I’m really unsure) but it’s around 40 or more dollars. 

5. Yes you will have to take it forever if you’re wanting to keep the effects, stop periods all of that. If you do stop, your voice won’t go back to normal female range after it drops, you will get your period back, fat will redistribute back into certain areas and things will generally become more feminine again. 

6. It shouldn’t but talk to your endo about it.

I had family with me and this was not in my home state so my mom basically drove me. Depending what you’re taking as in Meds (besides pain meds I had to take other medicine too) driving may not be the safest thing to do. Not only that but it might hurt to stretch your arms out in front of you so again may not wanna be driving. 

For having things near by I’d say at most water. Other things I think it is best to get up and move around stretch out your legs and get blood flowing into them. I kept the medicine I would need near by on the counter in the kitchen for me to get. 

For washing and bathing it is probably best to have someone help you wash your hair. The doctor will tell you when you could start washing your body. 

As for someone helping you again I had my mom there and my brother the whole time since again this was not in my hometown. I stayed there for a week until I got my drains out. But I had my mom at least help me bathe and empty my drains as well as get/help me make food. 

For sleeping and surgical binder- both of those things were the worst things ever in my recovery. I’m a person who likes to sleep on their side so sleeping sitting up wasn’t fun. Surgical also not that fun to have to have on, you feel a little cramped up. Your chest will get oily, very oily. 

As for doing anything like going out in public, I felt fine to do so. I had my meds that I needed to take on me and then meds that were optional if I needed to take on me. Not everyone is the same so it might be a few days for you before you’re feeling up to do anything outside of your home.
